editorNote: This week's picks lean toward measurement and honesty about results: a speculative-decoding paper argues that acceptance rate overstates speed, a medical-verification study finds models recognize duplicate trials yet still double count them, and a theory paper tracks how wide networks specialize. All claims here are drawn from the arXiv abstracts.

stories.headline: Higher acceptance in lossy speculative decoding does not mean faster decoding
stories.summary: Across twelve target-drafter pairs, the most relaxed settings averaged about 1.34× more accepted tokens per round but about 1.54× longer completions, mostly from longer reasoning traces. Rules that cut verifier rounds often lowered accuracy.
stories.whyItMatters: Acceptance rate alone can overstate speedup; the authors recommend reporting completion length and verifier rounds too.

sourceLinks.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding (arXiv)

stories.headline: DLite drafts without history to keep speculative decoding fast for agents
stories.summary: The authors report that agentic workloads can cut existing draft models' acceptance length by up to 80%. DLite reuses target-model hidden states and predicts locally without tracking full history, reporting up to 70% improvement over DSpark.
stories.whyItMatters: It targets the long, multi-turn contexts where current draft models degrade and KV-cache upkeep adds overhead.

sourceLinks.title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI (arXiv)

stories.headline: Distillation traces built around the student, not just the answer
stories.summary: ReDiST builds student-specific reasoning traces by revising correct drafts and repairing incorrect ones, scoring candidates with a frozen student-matched reader. It reports gains on QA benchmarks over answer-only and original-trace baselines.
stories.whyItMatters: The authors note that method rankings can differ between source and transfer benchmarks.

sourceLinks.title: Beyond the Answer: Student-Conditioned Trace Construction for Reasoning Distillation (arXiv)

stories.headline: LLMs recognize same-trial papers but still over-credit them as independent evidence
stories.summary: In 14 clinical families, GPT-5.5 reliably identified independent updates yet over-credited same-trial reports when aggregating; some other models showed a similar gap. A study-grouping instruction eliminated the over-crediting for GPT-5.5 in the later families.
stories.whyItMatters: The abstract's own line is 'Publication count is not study count': recognizing lineage does not guarantee correct aggregation.

sourceLinks.title: Recognizing Study Lineage Is Not Enough: Over-Crediting Same-Trial Evidence in LLM-Based Medical Verification (arXiv)

stories.headline: Pixel diffusion transformers get an adaptive parameterization and a high-frequency fix
stories.summary: MFlow learns to interpolate between clean-image and velocity prediction, with larger models preferring velocity. A frozen-backbone ConvRefiner trained adversarially restores the high-frequency statistics that pixel diffusion transformers lack, preserving FID.
stories.whyItMatters: It evaluates on ImageNet, UCF-101 video and large-scale text-to-image generation with competitive or improved results.

sourceLinks.title: Rethinking the design space of Vanilla Pixel Diffusion Transformers (arXiv)

stories.headline: A Gaussian picture of how wide networks begin to specialize
stories.summary: For wide two-layer networks trained on same-architecture targets, the authors describe the distribution of overlaps between learned and target features. Early training reduces to a few collective variables, and a 'quadratic shielding' mechanism speeds specialization.
stories.whyItMatters: It also estimates when specialization begins and how the activation function shapes the pattern.

sourceLinks.title: Mesoscopic learning dynamics of extensive-width neural networks (arXiv)
